intro_en: The Small Crater (Makhtesh Katan) is one of the most unique natural phenomena in Israel. In this segment of the Israel National Trail we cross the Small Crater and look out over it from several directions.
character_en: (For those walking north to south) The first part of the route is a fairly flat walk on a service track as far as the mouth of the Small Crater. From there, a gentle ascent to Ma'ale Eli, where there is a steep climb on a well-made path
pois_en: Middle Nahal Tzafit. Ma'ale Hatzera. The Small Crater. Ma'ale Eli. Mitzpe HaMakhtesh (the crater lookout)
important_en: When a flash-flood warning is issued for the streams of the south and east, hiking this segment is dangerous.
Until further notice, walking along the old road replaces the section through middle Nahal Tzafit and Ma'ale Hatzera, because of a safety problem in middle Nahal Tzafit.
Between the top of Ma'ale Eli and the overnight campsite in Nahal Akrabim, drinking water can be filled at a nearby military base.

It is not possible to reach the Nahal Akrabim campsite by vehicle; the road is physically blocked. On the other hand, although at the start of Road 227, coming from the Dimona-Oron road, there is signage prohibiting driving on the road, this route as far as the Nahal Akrabim campsite is not physically blocked. SPNI is working with the authorities to have the signage removed.
description_en:
From the overnight campsite above Nahal Tamar we head south. The trail descends to the channel of Nahal Tamar along a light-coloured earth embankment. When the phosphate quarry that once operated here was rehabilitated after its closure, the mining areas were filled with earth in an attempt to restore the land to its natural shape as it was before the mining.
Nahal Tamar is a short stream. Its source is about 4 km west of here, in the area of Metzad Tamar. There are several beautiful acacia trees in the channel. Note: the trail does not pass through the challenging canyon section of Nahal Tamar.
The trail crosses the channel and continues beside a layer of flint rock. On a low terrace we can see the remains of an ancient encampment site, a few remnants of walls and stone enclosures. We continue along the same contour, bypass a small dry waterfall and reach the top of a short ascent. On the way down it, we can make out the work invested in building it, but it has seen better days: a long time has passed since it was in use, and time and weathering have worn it down.
We reach the remains of a dirt road leading along a terrace above the channel of Nahal Tzafit, down into the channel. The Israel National Trail joins a black-marked trail heading up the stream.
After a few minutes' walk, outcrops of sandstone in yellow, red and purple begin to appear on both sides of the channel. Sandstone is a rock formed from the weathered material of ancient rocks that was carried away from the source rock and consolidated in a terrestrial environment into sandstone.
A lovely sight appears on the northern bank: at the top of a dry waterfall, on an overhanging rock ledge, grows an acacia tree. A little further on we pass trees growing in the channel, acacia and jujube.
After a short walk, water plants begin to appear on the left bank: reed, rush, seepweed (Suaeda) and Desmostachya grass. Along the channel from here to the big waterfall there are seeps and a high water table that sustain the water vegetation.
Before the trail begins to climb the left bank, a large acacia tree invites us to a break in its broad shade.
The trail makes a short climb and passes through rush bushes and tamarisk trees to the top of a beautiful dry waterfall; in the channel above the fall there are rock pools in the rock slabs. Here the trail leaves the stream channel and begins a long climb to the top of the northern cliff, a long and relatively steep climb of about 300 metres of vertical height.
In the last part of the ascent, the trail follows an ancient ascent route. From the top of the ascent we get a fine view from high above over the Tzafit channel.
The trail continues along the edge of a flat spur high above the channel, and after a short stretch of walking descends to a northern tributary of Nahal Tzafit. The trail crosses the tributary channel and meets a blue-marked trail coming from the area of Road 25 and Metzad Tamar, and continues with it south to Ma'ale Hatzera.
From here, it is a few minutes' walk to the crossing of the main channel of Nahal Tzafit. In the channel, a black-marked trail climbs right up upper Nahal Tzafit towards Ein Tzafit; we cross the channel and continue south to Ma'ale Hatzera. On its way to the top of Ma'ale Hatzera the trail climbs over spurs and crosses channels.
A moment before the trail reaches the rim of the crater we pass a trail junction, where the green-marked trail climbs left onto the ridge. It is recommended to follow the green trail a short distance to a fine viewpoint (a concrete circle with a low iron post rising from its centre marks the lookout point) that lets you take in the whole circumference of the crater at a single glance.
This is the place to pause briefly and explain about the craters (makhteshim) of the Negev, three of which the Israel National Trail passes through.
In the northern Negev there are five mountain ridges that are geological anticlines running from north-east to south-west. At this point we are standing on the crest of the easternmost of the five, the Hatzera Ridge.
A feature shared by all five ridge-anticlines is their asymmetry. The strata on the eastern flank rise to the crest of the anticline at a sharp angle, while on the western flank the dip of the strata is gentle. At the point where we stand on the Hatzera Ridge, looking out over the crater, this can be seen clearly and beautifully. The strata in the crater walls to our left are tilted, while the strata in the western crater wall, to our right, are almost horizontal. You can imagine a line extended from the end of each stratum on both sides of the crater, in the direction of its dip towards the centre of the crater. Every two imaginary lines extending from two matching strata on the two sides of the crater meet at the "crest of the anticline" above the crater.
Once upon a time, in an ancient geological era, after the anticline formed, the forces of erosion "ate away" the upper layers of hard limestone at the crest of the anticline and reached the layers beneath them, made of soft sandstone. Erosion cleared away the soft rocks quickly and easily, and so the crater was formed.
The Small Crater is drained by a single stream, Nahal Hatzera, into which flow several channels that look like the veins of a leaf. At the gate of the Small Crater, Nahal Hatzera exits eastwards from between the crater walls and empties into Nahal Zin, which continues to the Dead Sea.
The name "makhtesh" (mortar) was given by the pioneering desert hikers who reached the Small Crater in the 1940s. When they returned from their trip they wanted to describe what they had seen, and they used the word makhtesh to describe the great hollow whose shape reminded them of the vessel used for grinding coffee beans.
Back to the route: from the crater gate, the Israel National Trail continues with the red-marked trail towards the western wall of the crater, to Ma'ale Eli. We walk up the tributaries of Nahal Hatzera. The closer we get to the crater wall, the edge of the Nahal Hatzera drainage basin, the smaller the tributaries become. While crossing the crater, we pass several beautiful outcrops of multicoloured sandstone. It is worth looking around from time to time to see the crater walls closing around us like a rampart, 360 degrees.
Ma'ale Eli makes use of a spur descending from the crater wall to its floor. The climb up the spur is gentle at first and becomes steep further up; railings, steps and handholds assist the ascent. It is worth stopping from time to time to look at the rock section in the crater wall (and at the same time to steady your breathing and pulse...). At the top of the section you can make out cliffs of hard limestone, and beneath them the lower layers of sandstone in yellow, red, white and grey, where the crater wall is stepped and less steep.
The name Ma'ale Eli is borrowed from the name of the rod, the eli (pestle), used to grind the raw material inside the grinding vessel, that is, the makhtesh (mortar). Between one grinding and the next, the pestle rests inside the mortar, leaning on its rim, much like the ascent that "rests" on the wall of the Small Crater.
At the end of the strenuous climb, we reach the plateau. We walk along a red-marked dirt road to the overnight campsite.
Those who have not yet had their fill of the unique views of the crater can go to one last lookout over the crater from the Makhtesh lookout (Mitzpor HaMakhtesh). A green-marked road turning left off the Israel National Trail leads to the lookout and back.
Further along the road, at the head of Nahal Akrabim, there are two overnight campsites. The first is to the left of the road, and the second a few hundred metres further on, to the right of the road. From the campsites you can walk to a nearby hill topped with antennas, to fill water from a drinking-water tap installed for hikers beside the entrance to a military base.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, trail-marking coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
